module_title: Gin Distillation: From Ferment to Bottle

lessons.title: Building a Simple Pot Still from a Pressure Cooker and Copper Pipe
lessons.body: To build a pot still, you need a pressure cooker (6-8 litres), copper pipe (1/2 inch diameter, about 1.5 metres), a compression fitting to connect the pipe to the cooker lid, a bucket for cooling water, and a heat source (gas stove or charcoal). First, drill a hole in the pressure cooker lid that fits the compression fitting. Attach a short copper pipe (30 cm) vertically from the lidâthis is the column. Then connect a longer pipe (1 metre) at a 45-degree angle downward to act as the lyne arm. Finally, coil the remaining copper pipe into a spiral (the condenser) and place it inside a bucket. Connect the lyne arm to the top of the coil. Seal all joints with flour paste (mix flour and water to a thick paste) to prevent vapour leaks. Never use plastic or rubberâhot alcohol vapour dissolves them. Test your still by boiling water: if steam comes out only at the end of the coil, it's sealed. For cooling, fill the bucket with cold water and run a slow trickle of water in and out to keep it cool. This simple still can produce 2-4 litres of spirit per run. Safety: always distil outdoors or in a well-ventilated area, and never seal the output endâexplosion risk. Clean the copper with vinegar and salt before first use.

lessons.title: Fermenting a Sugar Wash with Local Yeast
lessons.body: A sugar wash is the cheapest and easiest ferment for gin. You need: 5 kg white sugar, 20 litres water, 100 g yeast (dry active yeast from a bakery or local market), 1 tablespoon lemon juice or 2 crushed vitamin C tablets, and 1 teaspoon yeast nutrient (optional but helps). Dissolve sugar in 5 litres of hot water, then top up to 20 litres with cold water. The temperature should be below 30Â°C before adding yeastâif it's too hot, it kills the yeast. Add lemon juice to make the wash slightly acidic (yeast likes pH 4-5). Sprinkle yeast on top and stir gently. Cover the bucket with a clean cloth and secure with a rubber bandâthis keeps flies out but lets gas escape. Keep it in a warm place (25-30Â°C) for 5-7 days. It will bubble vigorously for the first 3 days, then slow down. When bubbling stops and the wash tastes dry (not sweet), it's ready. In hot African climates, fermentation can finish in 3-4 days. If it smells like rotten eggs, add a teaspoon of yeast nutrient. Do not use bread yeast if you can get distiller's yeastâit produces less off-flavours. Strain the wash through a cloth before distilling to remove dead yeast. You should get about 20 litres of wash at 10-12% alcohol. This yields roughly 2 litres of pure alcohol after distillation.

lessons.title: First Distillation: Stripping Run and Collecting Low Wines
lessons.body: The stripping run is a fast, rough distillation to separate alcohol from water and solids. Pour your fermented wash into the pressure cooker, filling no more than two-thirds full to leave room for foaming. Add a teaspoon of cooking oil or a few pieces of clean copper to reduce foaming. Heat slowly at firstâif it boils too hard, foam will carry over into the condenser and contaminate your spirit. Once it starts dripping, increase heat slightly. Collect everything that comes out until the spirit coming off smells weak and watery (like wet cardboard). This is called 'low wines' and will be about 25-30% alcohol. Do not make cuts in this runâjust collect it all in one container. A 20-litre wash will take 2-3 hours to strip. Stop when the total volume collected is about 4-5 litres or when the temperature of vapour reaches 98Â°C. Discard the first 50 ml (foreshots) as it contains methanol and other toxinsâit smells like nail polish. After the run, clean your still with water. You can store low wines in a glass or stainless steel container for a few days before the spirit run. If you have a lot of wash, do multiple stripping runs and combine the low wines. This first run removes most water and solids, making the second distillation easier and cleaner.

lessons.title: Second Distillation: Making Cuts and Blending Hearts
lessons.body: The spirit run is where you make gin. Dilute your low wines to 40% alcohol with clean water (use a hydrometer to check). Pour into the still, filling no more than two-thirds. Heat very slowlyâthis run takes 4-6 hours. Collect the distillate in small jars (200-300 ml each). You will make three cuts: foreshots, heads, hearts, and tails. Foreshots: discard the first 50-100 ml (poisonous). Heads: collect the next 15-20% of the total alcoholâthese have sharp, solvent-like smells. Hearts: the middle portion, which smells clean and sweet. Tails: the last 20-30%, which smell oily and cardboard-like. To identify cuts, use your senses: dip a finger in each jar, rub, and smell. Hearts will smell pleasant. Collect hearts separately. You can blend a little heads and tails back into hearts for complexity, but only after diluting and tasting. A good rule: for 4 litres of low wines at 40%, you might get 1.5 litres of hearts at 60-70% alcohol. Keep records of temperatures and volumes. After blending, let the spirit rest for a day before flavouring. This second distillation concentrates alcohol and removes bad flavours. If you want a cleaner gin, do a third distillation.

lessons.title: Infusing Botanicals: Maceration vs. Vapor Infusion
lessons.body: Gin gets its flavour from juniper berries and other botanicals. Two main methods: maceration and vapour infusion. Maceration: soak botanicals directly in the spirit (or in the still during distillation). Use 20-30 g juniper berries, 5 g coriander seeds, 2 g angelica root, 1 g orris root, and optional citrus peel, cardamom, or lavender per litre of 40% spirit. Crush the botanicals lightly with a mortar and pestle. Soak for 24 hours, then distill. This gives a deep, earthy flavour. Vapour infusion: place botanicals in a mesh bag or basket in the vapour path above the boiling liquid. The hot alcohol vapour passes through them, extracting lighter, brighter flavours. This is how many premium gins are made. For a simple setup, tie a muslin bag of botanicals to the inside of the still's column. Use 15-20 g juniper per litre for vapour infusion. You can combine both: macerate half the botanicals and vapour-infuse the other half. In Africa, local botanicals like rooibos, hibiscus, baobab, or grains of paradise can replace or complement traditional ones. Start with small batches (1 litre) to test ratios. After infusion, you may need to redistill to avoid cloudiness. If you macerate and don't distill, the gin will be coloured and may go cloudy when chilled. For clear gin, always redistill after maceration.

lessons.title: Diluting, Filtering, and Bottling Gin at 40% ABV
lessons.body: After distillation, your gin is likely 60-70% alcohol. To bring it to 40% ABV (the standard for gin), use the formula: Volume of water to add = (Current ABV / Target ABV - 1) x Current Volume. For example, 1 litre at 65% needs (65/40 - 1) x 1 = 0.625 litres of water. Always add distilled or filtered water slowly while stirring. Use a hydrometer to check. If you overshoot, add a little more spirit. After dilution, the gin may become cloudy (called 'louche') due to oils from botanicals. Chill the gin to 0-4Â°C for 24 hours, then filter through coffee filters or a clean cotton cloth. This removes fatty oils and gives a clear spirit. For small batches, chill in a freezer then filter. Bottle in clean glass bottles with airtight caps. Rinse bottles with boiling water before filling. Fill to the neck, leaving 2 cm headspace. Label with date, ABV, and batch number. Store in a cool, dark place. Gin does not improve with age like wine, so drink within 1-2 years. For a professional look, use shrink caps and custom labels. If you sell, check local regulationsâmany countries require a licence for spirit production. Always test your final product: 40% ABV should burn slightly when rubbed on skin, and it should smell clean and juniper-forward.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum fill level for a pressure cooker when distilling?
quiz.explanation: Leaving headspace prevents foam and liquid from boiling over into the condenser.

quiz.q: Why should you never use plastic or rubber in a still?
options: A) They melt at low temperatures
B) Hot alcohol vapour dissolves them, contaminating the spirit
quiz.explanation: Alcohol is a solvent and will leach chemicals from plastic or rubber.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding lemon juice to a sugar wash?
options: B) To lower pH for yeast health
quiz.explanation: Yeast prefers a slightly acidic environment (pH 4-5).

quiz.q: How can you tell when a sugar wash is finished fermenting?
options: A) It stops bubbling and tastes dry
quiz.explanation: Lack of bubbling and a dry taste indicate sugar has been consumed.

quiz.q: What is the first distillate collected called, and why is it discarded?
quiz.explanation: Foreshots contain toxic methanol and other volatile compounds.

quiz.q: During a stripping run, when should you stop collecting?
options: A) When the spirit smells like wet cardboard
quiz.explanation: A weak, cardboard smell indicates alcohol is mostly exhausted.

quiz.q: What is the typical alcohol content of low wines from a stripping run?
quiz.explanation: Stripping runs concentrate alcohol to about 25-30% ABV.

quiz.q: In a spirit run, which cut is considered the best quality?
quiz.explanation: Hearts have the cleanest, sweetest flavour and aroma.

quiz.q: How can you identify the hearts cut by smell?
quiz.explanation: Hearts smell pleasant and fruity, without harsh notes.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between maceration and vapour infusion?
options: A) Maceration uses heat, vapour infusion uses cold
B) Maceration soaks botanicals in liquid, vapour infusion passes vapour through them
C) Maceration is for fruit, vapour infusion for spices
quiz.explanation: Maceration steeps botanicals in spirit; vapour infusion exposes them to hot vapour.

quiz.q: Which botanical is mandatory in gin?
quiz.explanation: Juniper is the defining flavour of gin.

quiz.q: Why might you redistill gin after maceration?
options: B) To make it clear and avoid cloudiness
quiz.explanation: Redistilling removes oils that cause cloudiness when chilled.

quiz.q: What is the formula to dilute spirit to a target ABV?
options: A) (Current ABV / Target ABV) x Volume
B) (Current ABV / Target ABV - 1) x Volume
C) (Target ABV / Current ABV) x Volume
D) (Target ABV - Current ABV) x Volume
quiz.explanation: This calculates the water needed to reach the desired strength.

quiz.q: What causes gin to become cloudy when diluted?
quiz.explanation: Essential oils from botanicals precipitate in cold, dilute alcohol.

quiz.q: How can you remove cloudiness from gin?
quiz.explanation: Chilling causes oils to clump, then filtration removes them.

quiz.q: What is the standard ABV for bottled gin?
quiz.explanation: 40% ABV is the minimum legal standard in many countries.

quiz.q: Why should you use distilled or filtered water for dilution?
options: B) To avoid off-flavours and cloudiness
quiz.explanation: Tap water may contain minerals that affect taste and clarity.

quiz.q: How should you clean bottles before filling?
quiz.explanation: Boiling water sanitises bottles and removes residues.

quiz.q: What is the recommended headspace when bottling gin?
quiz.explanation: A small headspace allows for expansion and prevents spills.

quiz.q: Why is it important to make cuts in the spirit run?
options: B) To separate good flavours from bad
quiz.explanation: Cuts isolate hearts from harsh heads and tails.

quiz.q: What temperature should you keep a sugar wash during fermentation?
quiz.explanation: Yeast is most active in this warm range.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a yeast nutrient?
options: B) To prevent off-smells and speed fermentation
quiz.explanation: Nutrients provide vitamins and minerals for healthy yeast.

quiz.q: How much juniper per litre is typical for vapour infusion?
quiz.explanation: 15-20 g per litre gives a balanced juniper flavour.

quiz.q: Which local African botanical can be used in gin?
quiz.explanation: Rooibos is a common African botanical with unique flavour.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a pot still?
options: B) Drill a hole in the pressure cooker lid
C) Seal joints with flour paste
quiz.explanation: The hole allows connection of the copper pipe to the lid.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to seal the output end of a still?
options: B) It can cause an explosion
quiz.explanation: Pressure builds up with no escape, leading to rupture.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for fermenting a sugar wash in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: This range balances speed and flavour.

quiz.q: How long should you macerate botanicals before distilling?
quiz.explanation: 24 hours extracts flavours without bitterness.

quiz.q: What is the typical yield of hearts from 4 litres of low wines at 40%?
quiz.explanation: About 1.5 litres of hearts at 60-70% is typical.

quiz.q: Why should you let gin rest after blending?
options: B) To allow flavours to meld
quiz.explanation: Resting integrates botanical flavours for a smoother taste.
